title: More Than 100 Nodules Took Over a Healthy Woman's Spleen, but Her Scans Showed Them Holding Still
text:
More Than 100 Nodules Took Over a Healthy Woman's Spleen, but Her Scans Showed Them Holding Still
A 46-year-old woman went in for a routine checkup feeling perfectly well. Her doctor felt an enlarged spleen, and imaging explained why: more than 100 solid and fluid-filled nodules had replaced at least 80% of the organ. Yet when her doctors lined up scans from 2021 through 2023, the lesions had barely changed.
The case, published May 10, 2026, in Cureus, comes from physicians affiliated with institutions in the United States, Colombia, and Honduras. They diagnosed splenic polyangiomatosis, also called diffuse splenic hemangiomatosis, an exceptionally rare and benign overgrowth of blood vessel channels.
A Routine Exam and a Spleen Full of Lumps
The woman had no significant medical history and no symptoms. Her vital signs were normal. The only abnormal finding was a non-tender enlarged spleen, with no swollen lymph nodes, skin blood vessel lesions, unusual bruising, or signs of liver disease.
When asked, she remembered being told about a similar finding years before, and she produced earlier imaging from an outside institution. A CT scan from September 2021 showed a spleen about 15.9 centimeters long, packed with countless irregular lesions. An ultrasound from January 2021 had described several simple cysts, though not to the extent seen on CT.
An MRI in December 2021 measured the spleen at about 15.6 centimeters, with innumerable solid and cystic lesions nearly replacing its tissue, the largest 2 to 3 centimeters across. A follow-up MRI in February 2023 counted more than 100 partly merging nodules occupying at least 80% of the spleen, which measured about 17 centimeters. Radiologists judged the overall appearance stable across the studies.
After the first MRI, radiologists listed several possibilities, including multiple littoral cell angiomas, atypical hemangiomas, lymphangiomas, and hamartomas, and recommended short-term follow-up imaging. The scans also showed mild fatty liver, while her pancreas, kidneys, adrenal glands and major abdominal vessels looked normal.
Ruling Out Cancer and Infection
A spleen riddled with nodules raises alarming possibilities, including lymphoma, cancer spread from elsewhere, abscesses and infections such as tuberculosis. The team worked through each one.
Her blood work was largely normal. White blood cells, hemoglobin and platelets were in range, as were C-reactive protein, sedimentation rate and lactate dehydrogenase. The only quirk was slightly enlarged red blood cells. Tests for hepatitis A, B and C, HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhea and H. pylori were negative.
The authors considered cancer effectively excluded because she had no fevers, night sweats or weight loss, normal blood counts, no enlarged lymph nodes and lesions that stayed stable over time, a pattern they describe as incompatible with untreated malignancy.
The imaging pattern also helped separate it from other benign spleen lesions. Littoral cell angioma often comes with anemia, low platelets, or autoimmune disease and tends to leave patches of normal spleen. Ordinary hemangiomas are usually few in number, and hamartomas and similar benign lesions typically appear alone. Her innumerable nodules, bright on certain MRI sequences and gradually brightening with contrast, fit polyangiomatosis best. The authors drew on published radiology guidance, including an algorithmic approach to spleen lesions laid out in RadioGraphics in 2022.
She also had a history of high-risk HPV infection, but the authors found no evidence linking HPV to vascular spleen lesions and considered it unrelated.
Watching Instead of Cutting
The diagnosis was made without a tissue sample. Doctors skipped a biopsy or spleen removal because she had no symptoms, remained stable, and did not need urgent surgery. She was referred to a general surgeon to discuss elective spleen removal versus continued monitoring.
That cautious approach matches the authors' summary of current practice. Spleen removal is generally reserved for people who develop symptoms, show growth or atypical imaging features, or need a definitive tissue diagnosis. For stable, symptom-free patients, periodic imaging is considered safe. The authors cited 2026 Canadian recommendations for incidental spleen findings in support.
She was encouraged to stay moderately active but to avoid high-impact and contact activities, because an enlarged spleen carries a theoretical risk of rupture with trauma. Spontaneous rupture in these benign vascular growths is exceedingly rare, the authors noted. Doctors also started vitamin D supplements.
A Condition Known Mostly From Single Cases
Splenic polyangiomatosis is poorly understood. Evidence points to either a congenital blood vessel malformation or a benign proliferative process, and its true incidence is unknown. Most of what is known comes from isolated reports, such as a 2025 description of the condition in an adolescent.
Most cases, like this one, are found by accident during imaging for something else, and benign vascular spleen lesions are being recognized more often as CT and MRI use grows.
The report has notable limits. It describes one patient, and without tissue confirmation, the diagnosis rests on imaging and clinical judgment. No imaging after February 2023 was described, so longer-term behavior remains uncertain.
People told they have an enlarged spleen or spleen lesions should discuss next steps with their doctor, since causes range from harmless to serious and only proper evaluation can tell them apart.
Key Questions Answered
What did doctors find?
A 46-year-old woman with no symptoms had an enlarged spleen containing more than 100 nodules that replaced at least 80% of its tissue.
What is splenic polyangiomatosis?
It is an exceptionally rare, benign overgrowth of blood vessel channels that can take over large parts of the spleen.
How did doctors rule out cancer?
She had no fevers, night sweats, or weight loss, normal blood counts, and no enlarged lymph nodes, and her lesions stayed stable on imaging from 2021 through 2023.
Was a biopsy done?
No. Because she was stable and symptom-free, doctors relied on imaging and lab results.
Will she need her spleen removed?
Not necessarily. She was referred to a surgeon to discuss elective removal versus monitoring. Removal is generally reserved for symptoms, growth, atypical imaging, or the need for a tissue diagnosis.
Are there activity restrictions?
Doctors advised avoiding high-impact and contact activities because of her enlarged spleen, while encouraging moderate exercise.
